questions.q: You want to see the shape of a single numeric column, such as flat prices: where most values sit and whether there is a long tail. Which chart fits best?
options: Pie chart
Line chart
Histogram
Scatter plot
questions.why: A histogram cuts the range into equal-width bins and counts the values in each, showing the distribution's shape. A scatter plot needs two numeric variables, and a line chart implies an order such as time.

questions.q: Order values are right-skewed: most orders are small, with a long tail of very large ones. How do the mean and median compare?
options: The median is above the mean
The mean is above the median
They are always equal
The mean is below the median because large values are rare
questions.why: The few very large values pull the mean up, while the median only cares about the middle value. Reasoning that rare large values "do not count much" is the trap; the mean is sensitive to every value's size.

questions.q: Eight sorted values: 10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 18, 40. Using NumPy's default quartiles, Q1 = 12.75 and Q3 = 16.5. Which values does a standard box plot draw as outlier dots?
options: None
Only 40
10 and 40
18 and 40
questions.why: IQR = 16.5 − 12.75 = 3.75. Fences: 12.75 − 1.5 × 3.75 = 7.125 and 16.5 + 1.5 × 3.75 = 22.125. Only 40 lies outside. 10 looks low but is above the lower fence; judging outliers by eye instead of by the 1.5 × IQR rule is the usual slip.

questions.q: A box plot of order values shows the median line near the bottom of the box, a long upper whisker and many dots above it. What does this suggest?
options: The data is symmetric with no unusual values
The box plot is broken; the median should be in the middle
The data is left-skewed, so the mean will sit below the median
The data is right-skewed with several unusually large orders, so the mean will sit above the median
questions.why: A median close to Q1 with a long upper tail means values bunch at the low end and stretch upwards: right skew. The median does not have to be in the centre of the box, and that asymmetry is exactly what the plot is showing you.

questions.q: Sixteen flat prices (₹ lakh): 28, 35, 42, 45, 48, 52, 55, 58, 61, 63, 67, 72, 78, 85, 96, 120. With bins of width 25 starting at 25, how many flats fall in the "50 to under 75" bin?
questions.why: 52, 55, 58, 61, 63, 67 and 72 give **7**. 78 belongs to the next bin and 48 to the one before. 5 is the count for the 25 to under 50 bin. Changing bin edges changes the bars, which is why you try more than one setting.

questions.q: A bar chart shows Branch A at 88% satisfaction and Branch B at 84%, with the y-axis running from 80% to 100%. B's bar looks half as tall as A's. What is the honest reading?
options: B's satisfaction is half of A's
B is performing badly enough to need urgent action
The gap is 4 percentage points; the truncated axis exaggerates it, so bar charts should start at zero
Bar heights always represent ratios, so the chart is correct
questions.why: Bars encode values by length, so starting the axis at 80% makes 8 versus 4 units of bar look like a 2 : 1 difference. Reading the bar heights as the ratio is exactly what a truncated axis tricks people into.

questions.q: A histogram of 60 delivery times looks smooth with one peak at 5 bins, but jagged with several peaks at 50 bins. What is the best conclusion?
options: The 50-bin version is right; more bins always show the truth
Histograms are unreliable, so use the mean instead
The data must contain several distinct groups
With only 60 values, many narrow bins mostly show noise; compare a few bin settings and trust features that persist
questions.why: Too many bins for the sample size leave only one or two values per bin, so random gaps look like structure; too few hide detail. Assuming more bins means more truth is the tempting error. Replacing the chart with a single summary throws away the shape altogether.

questions.q: Interview: "Why look at charts before building a model when you can just compute summary statistics?" Which answer is best?
options: Very different datasets can share the same mean, variance and correlation (Anscombe's quartet); plots reveal curves, outliers, typos and groups that summaries hide
Charts are mainly for presenting results to stakeholders
Summary statistics are usually computed incorrectly
Models cannot be trained without a histogram
questions.why: Anscombe's four datasets share x mean 9, y mean 7.50 and the same correlation and fitted line, yet look completely different. EDA is fast private looking to catch problems such as a ₹960 lakh typo, not presentation polish, which is the common misreading.
